rationale: This ethnographic and historical-geographical study examines how commercial forestry plantations disrupt native forests and natural water cycles in southern Chile and explores the resulting Mapuche environmental justice social movement. It concerns ambient watershed/hydrological scarcity and territorial protest rather than household or community water or sanitation service delivery (failing Criterion 1, E07), and it does not evaluate legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanisms governing water/sanitation service access or service-access outcomes (failing Criteria 2 and 4).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Excluded under both narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2 because the study focuses on ambient hydrological disruption from forestry plantations and indigenous social movement mobilization rather than household or community water or sanitation service access or service-governance mechanisms.

evidence_quotes.quote: we assess how forestry development has generated socio-spatial dynamics of environmental degradation and water scarcity in southern Chile.
recovering the native forest and its natural water cycles, which have been disrupted significantly by the increasing of forestry plantations.
We explore these dynamics of the Mapuche movement from an environmental justice approach.
